title: Landers and COD funnels
summary: How a COD nutra funnel turns a click into cash: prelander, order form, confirmation call, delivery and buyout. You learn the approval and buyout maths, how to raise both honestly, and how to keep fake and duplicate leads out.

lessons.title: The COD funnel from click to cash
objectives: By the end you can name every stage of a COD funnel and who controls it.
By the end you can turn payout and approval rate into a value per lead and a target CPL.
By the end you can write a COD numbers sheet before you spend.

steps.h: Why: a lead is not money yet
steps.p: In COD nutra you are usually paid per approved lead, not per form fill. Between your ad and your payout sit a call centre, a courier and a buyer who pays cash at the door. Each stage loses people. If you only watch cost per lead in Ads Manager, you can look like a winner there and still lose money at the network.

d.b: Leads cost money. Approved leads pay you.
d.s: Bought-out orders keep you paid next month.

steps.say: Here's why this lesson matters. In C O D, cash on delivery, nutra, you're usually paid per approved lead, not per form fill. Between your ad and your payout sit a call centre, a courier, and a buyer who pays cash at the door. Each stage loses people. Look at the headline: leads cost money, approved leads pay you. If you only watch cost per lead in Ads Manager, you can look like a winner there and still lose money at the network.

steps.p: This is the path from your ad to your payout. You control the first three boxes. The network, the call centre and the courier control the rest, but your traffic and your promises decide how well those later stages go. Tap through it once before reading on.
steps.say: This map is the path from your ad to your payout. Follow the arrows. Your ad leads to a prelander, then an order form. The lead goes to the network, which passes it to the call centre. Approved orders go to the courier, and the buyer pays cash. Meanwhile the call centre sends a status back as a postback, and approved leads become your payout. You control the first three boxes. But your traffic and your promises decide how well the later stages go.

steps.p: Every stage has an owner. Knowing who owns it tells you what you can fix yourself and what you can only ask about. Your biggest levers are the traffic you buy and the promises your ad and prelander make, because those shape every later stage.
steps.say: Every stage has an owner. Read down the table. The click and the prelander are yours, with levers like targeting, creative, and an honest, clear, priced page. The order form is you or the network, so aim for a valid phone and few fields. The confirmation call belongs to the call centre, delivery to the courier, and cash at the door to the buyer. Your biggest levers are the traffic you buy and the promises you make, because they shape every later stage.

steps.p: Example: 1,000 clicks give 60 order-form leads. 8 are invalid or duplicates, so 52 are valid. The call centre approves 27, which is 45% of all 60 leads. 17 buyers accept and pay at the door, a 63% buyout. Each step loses people, and only some of the losses are under your control.
steps.more: Approval rate is usually worked out on all leads, including trash, but some networks use valid leads only. Ask your network which one it uses, because the same traffic can show 45% or 52% depending on the definition. Buyout is normally paid orders divided by approved (or shipped) orders. Example: 17 ÷ 27 = 63%.
steps.say: Here's an example funnel. One thousand clicks give sixty order-form leads. Eight are invalid or duplicates, so fifty two are valid. The call centre approves twenty seven, which is forty five percent of all sixty leads. Seventeen buyers pay at the door, a sixty three percent buyout. One detail: some networks work out approval on valid leads only, so the same traffic could show fifty two percent. Ask your network which definition it uses.

steps.p: Because only approved leads pay, one raw lead is worth the payout times the approval rate. This is the most useful number in COD. It tells you the most a lead can cost before you lose money, and it changes every time approval moves.
steps.more: Example: payout $14 per approved lead and 45% approval. $14 × 0.45 = $6.30. If you pay $6.30 per lead you break even. Pay $7 and you lose $0.70 on every lead on average, even though 45 out of 100 leads paid you $14. Many beginners compare their CPL with the $14 payout and think they have a lot of room. They do not.
steps.say: This is the most useful number in C O D. Because only approved leads pay, one raw lead is worth the payout per approved times the approval rate. For example, a fourteen dollar payout at forty five percent approval gives six dollars thirty per lead. Pay six thirty and you break even. Pay seven dollars and you lose seventy cents on every lead on average. Many beginners compare their C P L, cost per lead, with the full fourteen dollars and think they have lots of room. They don't.

steps.p: Example: payout $14, approval 45%, and you want to keep a 25% margin. Value per lead is $6.30. Keep 25% and you can pay up to $6.30 × 0.75 = $4.73 per lead. That is your target CPL. Your target CPA per approved lead is $14 × 0.75 = $10.50.
steps.say: Now let's find a target C P L. In this example, the payout is fourteen dollars, approval forty five percent, and you want to keep a twenty five percent margin. Value per lead is six dollars thirty. Keep twenty five percent, and you can pay up to six thirty times zero point seven five, about four dollars seventy three per lead. That's your target C P L. Your target C P A, cost per approved lead, is fourteen times zero point seven five, ten dollars fifty.

steps.p: Try it with the calculator. The field for leads that convert stands for the approval rate here. Enter the payout, the approval rate and your margin, then check the answer. Change approval to 35% afterwards and watch how much the line drops.

At forty five percent, it's worth six dollars thirty. At sixty percent, eight dollars forty. Same ads, same C P L, very different business. Approval is a multiplier on everything.

steps.p: Example: write these seven lines before launch, from a $14 payout, a 45% expected approval and a 25% margin. They feed every rule in this school. The kill and scale lines use approved leads, the same rule card you learned in Foundations, just counted on the stage that pays.
steps.more: Why 'lower of 1.5 × target and break-even'? 1.5 × $10.50 is $15.75, which is above the $14 payout. A rule that lets you keep paying $15 for something that pays $14 is not a rule, so the break-even wins. Approvals arrive late in COD, so Module 5 shows how to apply these lines while statuses are still pending.
steps.say: Here's your C O D numbers sheet, an example from a fourteen dollar payout, forty five percent approval and twenty five percent margin. Break-even C P A, fourteen dollars. Target C P A, ten fifty. Scale line, zero point eight times target, eight forty. Zero-lead kill, spend two times target with no leads, twenty one dollars. The C P A kill line is the lower of one point five times target and break-even. One point five times ten fifty is above the payout, so break-even wins, fourteen dollars. Break-even C P L six thirty, target C P L four seventy three.

steps.p: These mistakes all come from treating a lead like a sale. Check your own sheet against the left column. If you are making any of them, your real margin is smaller than you think, and scaling will make that worse.

steps.h: Compliance: only legal, honest orders pay
steps.p: Your numbers mean nothing if the product cannot legally be sold or advertised in the geo. Many countries require health products and supplements to be registered, and some require ads to be approved first. Ask the advertiser before you plan a budget.

lessons.title: Prelanders that pre-qualify buyers
objectives: By the end you can explain why the best COD prelander is not the one with the most leads.

steps.h: Why: the prelander sets the phone call
steps.p: A prelander is the page between your ad and the order form. In COD its job is not the biggest number of form fills. Its job is form fills from people who will say yes on the phone and pay at the door. A page that hides the price or overpromises fills the call centre with people who were never going to buy.

d.b: Sell the call, not the click
d.s: Every promise on the page is checked by a phone call and a cash payment.

steps.p: The left column is common in nutra and it is the fastest way to lose ad accounts, network trust and approval rate. The right column gets fewer leads per click but more approved ones, and you can run it for months without hiding anything.

b.title: Pre-qualifying prelander
items: What it is, what to expect

steps.say: Compare the two columns. On the left, the hype prelander: a fake news-site masthead, cure and miracle promises, the price hidden until the call, and fake comments and fake doctors. It's common in nutra, and it's the fastest way to lose ad accounts, network trust and approval rate. On the right, the pre-qualifying page: labelled Advertisement, what it is and what to expect, price, delivery and C O D shown, and real, permitted testimonials only. Fewer leads per click, but more approved ones.

steps.p: Pick the format that fits your traffic and your offer, not the one that looks cleverest. Every format below can be honest or dishonest. Module 3 covered angles; here we care about how each format affects approval and buyout.
d: Labelled advertorial|a story with clear 'Advertisement' label
Product info page|what it is, how to use, price
Short quiz|who it suits and who it does not
Video page|a person explains the product
Direct to order|no prelander, for warm or simple offers
steps.say: Here are prelander formats that fit C O D. A labelled advertorial, a story with a clear Advertisement label. A product info page, covering what it is, how to use it, and the price. A short quiz on who it suits and who it doesn't. A video page where a person explains the product. Or direct to order, with no prelander, for warm or simple offers. Pick the format that fits your traffic and offer. Every one of these can be honest or dishonest.

steps.p: This order works for most COD supplements. Each block answers one question the call-centre agent would otherwise have to answer, so the call is shorter and the yes is firmer. Keep each block short on mobile.
d: What the product is (and is not)
steps.say: This order works for most C O D supplements. Follow the flow. A hook that matches the ad. The everyday problem, in plain words. What the product is, and what it isn't. Realistic expectations and how to use it. Then price, delivery, and pay on delivery. And finally the order button. Each block answers a question the call-centre agent would otherwise have to answer, so the call is shorter and the yes is firmer.

steps.p: Example: $300 spend and 1,000 clicks on each page. The hype page wins on CPL. The honest page wins on cost per approved lead, which is the number that pays. If you only read Ads Manager, you would pick the wrong page.
steps.more: Maths: hype page 80 × 30% = 24 approved, $300 ÷ 24 = $12.50. Honest page 60 × 50% = 30 approved, $300 ÷ 30 = $10.00. Against a $10.50 target the honest page passes and the hype page does not. Buyout usually widens the gap further, because buyers who were promised a miracle refuse the parcel. These figures are illustrative; your own test decides.
steps.say: Here's an example with three hundred dollars spend and one thousand clicks on each page. The hype page gets eighty leads at three dollars seventy five, but only thirty percent approval, so twenty four approved at twelve dollars fifty each. The honest page gets sixty leads at five dollars, with fifty percent approval, so thirty approved at ten dollars each. Against a ten fifty target, the honest page passes. These figures are illustrative, and buyout usually widens the gap further.

steps.p: To compare pages fairly, count approved leads per 1,000 clicks. It combines the page's lead rate and the call centre's approval in one number. Higher is better, as long as the cost per click is the same for both pages.
steps.more: Example: honest page 1,000 × 6% × 50% = 30. Hype page 1,000 × 8% × 30% = 24. When the ads and audience are the same, CPC is the same, so the page with more approved per 1,000 clicks also has the lower cost per approved lead.
steps.say: To compare pages fairly, count approved leads per thousand clicks. Multiply one thousand clicks by the lead rate and by the approval rate. For example, the honest page: one thousand times six percent times fifty percent is thirty. The hype page: one thousand times eight percent times thirty percent is twenty four. When the ads and audience are the same, the C P C, cost per click, is the same, so the page with more approved per thousand also has the lower cost per approved lead.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. Split traffic evenly between two pages in the same ad set or with identical ad sets. Judge on cost per approved lead after statuses have arrived. A page that wins on CPL but loses on approval is a loser.

steps.say: These are starting rules for prelander tests. Under thirty leads per page, keep running. While statuses are pending, wait until about ninety percent of leads have a final status. If one page is fifteen percent or more cheaper per approved lead, keep it and pause the other. Under fifteen percent apart, keep the simpler, more honest page. And if both are over fourteen dollars per approved, fix the offer or angle, not the page. A page that wins on C P L but loses on approval is a loser.

steps.p: Each of these makes the form fill easier and the phone call harder. If your approval rate is below the network's average for the geo, check your page for these before blaming the call centre.

steps.say: Each of these mistakes makes the form fill easier and the phone call harder. Hiding the price, so the buyer hears it first on the call and says no. Overpromising, so they refuse the parcel when results feel ordinary. Fake urgency, like countdowns that reset, which is deceptive. Message mismatch between ad and page. And no 'who it's not for', so the wrong buyers order. If your approval is below the network's average, check your page before blaming the call centre.

steps.p: There is no single right answer. A short form brings more leads, including more careless ones. A longer form filters out people who are only curious. You decide by testing, and you judge on approved leads.

steps.h: Example: form test on approved leads

Keep testing or keep the version the call centre prefers. Ask the network which form gives them fewer no-answers and faster calls; that is useful data you cannot see yourself.

lessons.title: Call-centre approval: what you control
objectives: By the end you can explain what happens on a confirmation call and each lead status.
By the end you can find the traffic, page and timing causes of low approval.
By the end you can apply approval rules per ad set and talk to the network with data.

steps.p: Approval rate is the share of your leads the call centre confirms. Raise it from 40% to 50% and every lead is worth 25% more, without changing your CPL. Most affiliates cannot touch the call centre, but they control many of the things that decide how the call goes.

d.s: Example: from 40% to 50% on the same leads.

steps.say: Approval rate is the share of your leads the call centre confirms. Look at the headline: plus ten points of approval is plus twenty five percent value. For example, going from forty to fifty percent on the same leads makes every lead worth twenty five percent more, without changing your C P L, cost per lead. Most affiliates can't touch the call centre, but they control many of the things that decide how the call goes.

steps.p: Example: payout $14. At 40% approval one lead is worth $5.60. At 50% it is worth $7.00. That is $1.40 more per lead, a 25% increase. At a $5 CPL you go from a $0.60 margin to a $2.00 margin per lead.
steps.say: Let's work the example. The payout is fourteen dollars. At forty percent approval, one lead is worth five dollars sixty. At fifty percent, it's worth seven dollars. That's one dollar forty more per lead, a twenty five percent increase. At a five dollar C P L, your margin goes from sixty cents to two dollars per lead. Same traffic, much better business.

steps.h: What a confirmation call sounds like
steps.p: This is a typical, honest confirmation call, shown as text. The agent confirms the order, the price and the address, and gives the buyer a clear chance to say no. Your prelander should make every answer here unsurprising.

messages.text: Good afternoon, is this Ada? You ordered a joint-care supplement today.
It is one pack at the price on the page, paid on delivery. Is that still fine?
Yes. How long will it take?
2 to 4 days. Can you confirm your address and a landmark?
Thank you. Your order is confirmed.

steps.say: Here's a typical, honest confirmation call, shown as text. The agent checks it's Ada, and confirms the order: one pack at the price on the page, paid on delivery. Ada asks how long it takes, two to four days. The agent confirms her address and a landmark, near the pharmacy, then confirms the order. Notice the buyer gets a clear chance to say no. Your prelander should make every answer here unsurprising.

steps.p: Networks report each lead with a status. Names differ by network, so check yours, but the meaning is usually close to this. Only approved leads pay. Callback leads can still become approved, which is why you wait before judging.
steps.say: Networks report each lead with a status. Names differ, but the meaning is usually close to this table. Approved, the order was confirmed on the call, and it pays you. Pending or callback, not reached yet, will retry, so not yet. Rejected or cancelled, reached but said no. Trash or invalid, a wrong number, fake or joke. Duplicate, the same buyer already ordered. Only approved leads pay. And callback leads can still become approved, which is why you wait before judging.

Right audience|age, region and language match the offer

Timing|ads run when the call centre can call soon

steps.h: Example: should you run ads at night?
steps.p: Example: CPL is $4.20 at night and $4.80 by day. Night leads look cheaper in Ads Manager but cost more per approved lead. Against a $10.50 target, day passes and night is close to the line.
steps.more: Maths: day $4.80 ÷ 0.48 = $10.00. Night $4.20 ÷ 0.36 = $11.67. Before you cut night hours, check you have enough leads in each window (we use 30+ as a starting minimum). Ad scheduling options differ by platform; on Meta, scheduling has historically needed a lifetime budget. We are not certain this is current; check the current Ads Manager before relying on it.

Against a ten fifty target, day passes. Check you have thirty or more leads per window first. lessons.title: Buyout: why delivered-and-paid keeps you paid
objectives: By the end you can explain why the advertiser cares about buyout even when you are paid on approval.
By the end you can work out an advertiser's break-even buyout from simple costs.
By the end you can spot traffic that approves well but buys out badly, and act on it.

steps.h: Why: approval pays you, buyout keeps you paid
steps.p: Most COD deals pay you when a lead is approved. The advertiser only earns when the buyer pays at the door. If your approved orders are refused at delivery, the advertiser loses money on them. Sooner or later that comes back to you as a lower payout, a smaller cap or a closed offer.

d.b: Your payout is funded by buyout
d.s: Low buyout traffic gets cut, even when approval looks fine.

steps.say: Most C O D, cash on delivery, deals pay you when a lead is approved. But the advertiser only earns when the buyer pays at the door. Look at the headline: your payout is funded by buyout. If your approved orders are refused at delivery, the advertiser loses money on them. Sooner or later that comes back to you as a lower payout, a smaller cap, or a closed offer, even when approval looks fine.

steps.p: Example: 100 approved orders. 96 are shipped; the rest have stock or address problems. 82 are reached by the courier. 64 buyers pay. Buyout here is 64 of 100 approved, or 64%. Every refused parcel still cost the advertiser product, delivery and your payout.
steps.say: Here's an example of what happens after approval. One hundred approved orders. Ninety six are shipped, the rest have stock or address problems. Eighty two are reached by the courier. And sixty four buyers pay. So buyout here is sixty four of one hundred, or sixty four percent. Every refused parcel still cost the advertiser product, delivery and your payout.

steps.p: Example: a simplified view of one approved order. The advertiser pays all these costs on every approved order but only gets the price when the buyer pays. Real models also count returns and restocking; this is enough to see the problem.
steps.say: This table is a simplified example of the advertiser's maths for one approved order. The price paid at the door is thirty nine dollars, but only if bought out. Product cost, five dollars on every shipped order. Delivery and the C O D fee, six dollars, paid even if refused. Call centre and admin, two dollars. Your payout, fourteen dollars on approval. Total cost, twenty seven dollars before any revenue. Real models also count returns and restocking, but this is enough to see the problem.

steps.p: Divide the total cost per approved order by the price. Below that buyout, the advertiser loses money on your traffic. Example: $27 ÷ $39 = 69%. At 64% buyout they earn $24.96 per approved order and spend $27, a loss of about $2 each.
steps.more: Example maths: $39 × 0.64 = $24.96 revenue per approved order. $24.96 − $27 = −$2.04. At 75% buyout: $39 × 0.75 = $29.25, so $29.25 − $27 = +$2.25. These numbers are illustrative; real costs vary a lot by product, courier and country. The point is that a few points of buyout decide whether the advertiser can keep paying you.
steps.say: Here's the advertiser's break-even buyout. Divide the cost per approved order by the price. In this example, twenty seven divided by thirty nine is sixty nine percent. At sixty four percent buyout, they earn twenty four dollars ninety six and spend twenty seven, a loss of about two dollars each. At seventy five percent, they make about two dollars twenty five. These numbers are illustrative, but a few points of buyout decide whether the advertiser can keep paying you.

steps.p: Example, using the costs above. Each step of 10 points in buyout moves the advertiser's result by about $3.90 per approved order. This is why networks ask about traffic quality and why they compare your buyout with other affiliates in the same geo.
steps.say: Look at these bars, using the same example costs. At fifty five percent buyout, the advertiser loses five dollars fifty five per approved order. At sixty five percent, minus one sixty five. At seventy five, plus two twenty five. At eighty five, plus six fifteen. Each ten point step moves the result by about three dollars ninety. That's why networks ask about traffic quality and compare your buyout with other affiliates in the same geo.

steps.p: Buyout is decided at the door, days after the click. These are the factors that usually matter. The first three are in your hands as an affiliate; the rest are the advertiser's, but you can ask about them.
d: Honest expectations|buyer gets what the ad promised
Right regions|only where the courier delivers
Clear price|no surprise at the door
Fast delivery|less time to change their mind
steps.say: Buyout is decided at the door, days after the click. Here are the factors that usually matter. Honest expectations, so the buyer gets what the ad promised. Right regions, only where the courier delivers. A clear price, so there's no surprise at the door. These first three are in your hands. Then fast delivery, a reminder message, and easy rescheduling are the advertiser's, but you can ask about them.

steps.h: A delivery reminder the advertiser sends
steps.p: Many advertisers send a short reminder before delivery. You do not send it, but knowing it exists helps you ask the right question. If your network's advertiser has no reminder step, ask whether they plan one.

messages.text: Hello Ada, your joint-care supplement order arrives Thursday. Price as agreed, pay on delivery. To change the day, reply 1.
No problem. We will call you to agree a new day.

steps.say: Many advertisers send a short reminder before delivery. In this example S M S, Ada is told her order arrives Thursday, price as agreed, pay on delivery, and to reply one to change the day. She replies one, and they'll call to agree a new day. You don't send this yourself, but knowing it exists helps you ask the right question.
